implementation_notes: System.Threading.Channels is the .NET-blessed producer/consumer primitive: Channel.CreateBounded declares the capacity and BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait (the default) makes WriteAsync wait for space, while TryWrite returns false immediately, and consumers use ReadAllAsync/ReadAsync. Because the hand-off is asynchronous, worker count and thread pool are decoupled from the buffer - the channel bound is the load-levelling control. The channel replaces the classic queue-plus-monitor structure entirely; hand-rolled BlockingCollection code is only justified when consumers are synchronous threads that cannot be made async.
pitfalls: Channel.CreateUnbounded removes the bound and with it the whole point; the default capacity must be chosen deliberately.
FullMode DropWrite/DropOldest/DropNewest turn the channel into a shedder - legitimate for telemetry, wrong for work that must not be lost, and silently so unless the itemDropped callback is wired up.
SingleReader/SingleWriter flags are promises: setting them while several tasks actually read or write produces undefined consumption order and lost messages.
Writer.Complete() must be called (and consumers must observe completion) or ReadAllAsync never finishes and shutdown hangs.

variants.name: BlockingCollection<T> with a bounded capacity and consuming threads
variants.implementation_notes: BlockingCollection<T> provides blocking and bounding capabilities over any IProducerConsumerCollection: constructing it with a boundedCapacity makes Add block when full, Take blocks while empty, and GetConsumingEnumerable() gives the worker loop; CompleteAdding() ends it. This is the pre-Channels idiom and still the right choice when workers are plain threads, when a custom backing collection (priority, stack) is required, or on targets without System.Threading.Channels. The classic queue-plus-monitor code is never needed - the collection owns the synchronization.
pitfalls: Constructing BlockingCollection<T>() without boundedCapacity gives an unbounded queue and no backpressure at all.
A consumer that throws inside GetConsumingEnumerable loses that item (it is already removed); retry/dead-letter handling has to happen inside the loop.
Long-running workers need TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning or they occupy thread-pool threads while blocked in Take.
